approach: A prospective observational study design involving 48 NSCLC patients. Gut microbiota was assessed via 16S rRNA gene sequencing (V1-V2 region) of pre-treatment fecal samples, analyzing alpha-diversity (Chao1, Shannon index), beta-diversity, and taxonomic composition (LEfSe analysis). Functional potential was predicted using PICRUSt2. Tumor immune status was evaluated using multiplex immunofluorescence staining for CD8+, PD-1+, CTLA-4+, FOXP3+ cells, etc. Clinical outcomes (PFS, OS, ORR) were analyzed using Kaplan-Meier curves and Cox proportional hazards models. To address treatment selection bias between I-N alone and I-N + chemotherapy groups, inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) was employed. Subgroup analyses were stratified by gut microbiota diversity (high vs. low based on median Shannon index).

contribution_and_limits.contribution: Provides evidence that baseline gut microbiota diversity predicts the efficacy of I-N monotherapy in NSCLC and identifies a subgroup (low diversity) that may benefit from adding chemotherapy.
contribution_and_limits.limits: The study is limited by a small sample size (N=48), which reduces statistical power for subgroup and taxa-level comparisons. It is an observational study, so causality cannot be established. Confounding factors such as diet, comorbidities, and detailed concomitant medications were not fully controlled. The findings are hypothesis-generating and require validation in larger, diverse cohorts.

key_findings.finding: High baseline gut microbiota alpha-diversity was significantly associated with longer progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS). High diversity also correlated with increased density of CD8+ TILs, particularly PD-1+CD8+ T cells.
Enrichment of SCFA-producing bacteria (e.g., Lachnospiraceae, Coprococcus, Eubacterium) and metabolic pathways related to peptidoglycan biosynthesis and NOD-like receptor signaling.

key_findings.conditions: Patients treated with I-N plus chemotherapy
key_findings.finding: No significant association was found between gut microbiota diversity/composition and treatment efficacy. Low-diversity patients showed a clear PFS benefit from adding chemotherapy compared to I-N alone, whereas high-diversity patients did not show such an advantage.
Antibiotic use within 1 month prior to treatment was independently associated with significantly shorter PFS and OS, regardless of whether chemotherapy was added.

problem_or_question: To determine if baseline gut microbiome features can serve as biomarkers to predict response to dual checkpoint blockade (I-N) in NSCLC and to assess whether these features can help identify patients who would benefit from adding chemotherapy to the regimen, thereby optimizing patient selection and personalized treatment strategies.
research_scope: Advanced non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients treated with dual checkpoint blockade (ipilimumab + nivolumab, I-N), with or without chemotherapy. The study focuses on the association between baseline gut microbiome characteristics and treatment outcomes, as well as the tumor immune microenvironment.
work_summary: This prospective cohort study investigated whether baseline gut microbiota diversity and composition could predict the efficacy of ipilimumab plus nivolumab (I-N) therapy in advanced NSCLC and guide the decision to add chemotherapy. The study enrolled 48 patients who received fecal samples for 16S rRNA sequencing and tumor tissues for multiplex immunofluorescence staining before treatment initiation. Researchers analyzed the correlation between gut microbiome alpha-diversity/composition and clinical outcomes (PFS, OS, ORR), as well as tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs). The results indicated that high gut microbiota diversity and the presence of short-chain fatty acid (SCFA)-producing bacteria were associated with improved PFS and greater CD8+ T-cell infiltration specifically in patients receiving I-N monotherapy. In contrast, these associations were not observed in patients receiving I-N combined with chemotherapy, where low-diversity patients appeared to benefit more from the addition of chemotherapy. Additionally, prior antibiotic use was independently associated with shorter survival across all regimens.
